newsitem.title: UK: British economy heading for soft landing - survey.
newsitem.headline: British economy heading for soft landing - survey.

text.p: Consumer confidence in Britain jumped sharply after the May 1 election but optimism that household finances will improve in the future levelled off, a leading consumer survey said on Thursday.

Business Strategies Ltd (BSL), an independent research company, said the findings in its latest Consumer Market Quarterly Bulletin suggest that the economy was in for a 'soft landing' -- a gentle slowdown in the economy.

"The windfall cash (from building society conversion) has arrived, people are spending it or saving it and there is nothing to suggest we are in for a hard landing or there is any threat of recession," said David Fell, director at BSL.
He said optimism about the economy reached its highest level since the survey began in the early 1980s thanks, in part, to post-election cheer.

"Post-election euphoria seems to have played a significant part in the results. The regions where optimism about the economy has increased most dramatically are those in which Labour support has traditionally been strongest -- the north, the north-west, Scotland and Wales."

After 18 years in opposition, Labour won the May 1 election with a huge majority. Fell said economic confidence has tended to pick up after elections but never so dramatically, although figures for the last change of government in 1979 were not available.
He said the strong pick-up in optimism could not be accounted for by the good run of economic data alone.
"Take the south east. Here, unemployment has fallen steadily all year and is now below 4.0 percent yet, in the latest survey, the views of the region's consumers have barely changed since last time."
In the south east the balance of optimists over pessimists rose by eight points in the three-month period, while in Scotland it rose by 17 points and by 19 points in the north.
But, surprisingly, while economic confidence rose dramatically in the second quarter, households are not expecting any further improvement in their finances.

Millions of households have seen their finances boosted in the last three months by windfall cash from building societies converting into banks. But these one-off payments are coming to an end and households are adjusting their behaviour accordingly.

"Crucially, the survey shows that in all regions saving is becoming more attractive. Sixty percent of consumers think that now is a good time to save. This compares with 48 percent a year ago and a long term average of 50 percent," Fell said.
He said the survey suggested talk of an unsustainable boom was misplaced and the central bank should make no move on interest rates for the time being.
"The Bank of England should hang fire on interest rate rises and wait for the blip in confidence to evaporate and return to the path it was previously on," he added.
The Bank of England's monetary policy committee meets next week to consider the current 6.75 percent interest rate.
